title: Carryover ladder
purpose: Take the voice you like from easy, automatic speech into longer, freer talking, one rung at a time.
instructions: Start on the lowest rung: speech so automatic you can pay attention to how you sound, not what to say.
Use your practice voice for the whole rung.
Move up only when the rung feels comfortable and your voice stays steady through it.
If a rung is too much, step down and spend longer on the one before.

primary_cue.text: Keep your practice voice, easily, for the whole rung.

cues.text: Keep your practice voice, easily, for the whole rung.
Step down a rung and give it more time.

practice_task.prompt_text: Use your practice voice for this rung of the ladder.

ladder.text: Say the months of the year.
Count on from fifty to seventy-five.
Say your name, an address and a phone number (made-up ones are fine, or record privately).
Read a few short sentences aloud: a news story, a recipe, a shop's opening hours.
Talk for one minute about anything: your morning, a film, what's for dinner.
Say the short things you really say: ordering a coffee, answering the phone, greeting a neighbour.
Read a few paragraphs of a book aloud.
Chat for a few minutes with someone you know well.

check_questions.text: Could you keep your practice voice easily through this rung?

dose_guidance.text: Little and often works best: a few minutes at a time, several times a day, builds the habit without tiring your voice. There's no set time per rung, and Lilt only logs what you choose to.

progression_rule.text: Lilt offers the next rung after two sessions in a row where you say it went easily and steadily.
progression_rule.source_basis: Moving up only once a step feels easy is common practice in voice training; two sessions in a row is Lilt's own setting.

expected_observations: Progress is rarely steady. Some rungs take much longer than others.
common_misunderstandings: Reading well doesn't mean your voice will hold in conversation yet.
stop_conditions: Anything hurts, feels tight or scratchy, or your voice turns hoarse: that usually means too much, too soon.
Rest your voice and come back another day, starting smaller.

Hoarseness that lasts more than about three weeks, sudden voice loss or pain needs a GP or primary care doctor, who can have your vocal folds looked at. A speech and language therapist who works with voices can help with technique.
Any pain or discomfort: stop, and step back a rung next time.
adaptations: Build your own ladder from the situations in your life.
limitations: Written for Lilt for practising on your own. Lilt can't check your technique, and it doesn't replace a speech and language therapist.
The last two rungs happen away from Lilt; it only knows what you tell it.
